name: Mongolian beef — economical protein (beef or chicken)

source.author: Pasted recipe text (English)
source.notes: A velveting-technique stir-fry: beef (or chicken) marinated with baking soda + cornstarch + egg white for tenderness, dusted in cornstarch, flash-fried at a moderate 120-140°C, then tossed in a soy-brown sugar-Shaoxing wine sauce with garlic, ginger, capsicum and spring onion. Analyzed with BEEF chuck as the protein (as listed first); the recipe's own 'economical protein' framing explicitly allows swapping in chicken breast/thigh instead — that swap would cut fat roughly in half and raise protein density noticeably (see suggested_mods). Rice ('to serve') is not quantified in the post, so it's excluded from the macros here — add it separately when logging a meal. Oil absorption during flash-frying is an estimate (lower-temp velvet-frying absorbs less than deep-frying, but it's still a fried step). Not quantified: optional baking-soda 'extra tender' pre-step (washed off before marinating, so it doesn't add macros). Estimate.

serving_desc: ≈310 g cooked (batch ÷4), beef version — not including rice

ingredients.item: beef (chuck or topside), sliced thin against the grain
ingredients.note: or swap to chicken breast/thigh — see suggested_mods

ingredients.qty: extra, as needed — shake off excess

steps: Slice the protein thin against the grain.

Mix with baking soda, cornstarch, egg white, soy sauce, white pepper and oil; marinate ~30 min (optionally, pre-tenderize raw meat with baking soda alone for ~40 min, then rinse and pat dry before marinating as above).
Dust lightly in extra cornstarch, shaking off excess.
Flash-fry in batches in oil at ~120-140°C until just cooked; drain.
Stir-fry the capsicum briefly, then the ginger and garlic until fragrant.
Add the combined sauce ingredients (soy sauce, brown sugar, water, Shaoxing wine) and simmer until glossy; thicken with the cornstarch slurry if needed.
Return the protein and spring onions to the pan; toss to coat in the sauce.

batch_totals.note: Whole dish (4 servings), BEEF version, excluding rice. Three separate oil additions (marinade + flash-fry + stir-fry, ~56 g total) plus beef chuck's own fat make this fattier than most of your library's chicken dishes; soy sauce x2 + Shaoxing wine drive the sodium.

him.verdict: Decent protein (~28.7 g/serving) but with meaningfully more fat than your typical rotation dish — ~30 g/serving, from beef chuck's own marbling plus three separate oil additions (marinade, flash-fry, stir-fry). That's ~6.4 g protein per 100 kcal, below your usual chicken dishes' density. Sodium is also high (~679 mg/serving) from the double soy sauce + Shaoxing wine. The capsicum and spring onion add a real vitamin-C boost. Swapping to chicken breast (the recipe's own suggested alternative) would be the single biggest lever — it would cut fat roughly in half while keeping protein similar or higher.
flags: ~28.7 g protein / 446 kcal (~6.4 g protein per 100 kcal — below your usual chicken-dish density)
~30 g fat/serving — beef chuck's own fat + 3 separate oil additions
high sodium (~679 mg/serving) — double soy sauce + Shaoxing wine
~6 g added sugar/serving (brown sugar in the sauce)
good vitamin C from capsicum + spring onion; rice not included in these macros
suggested_mods: Swap to chicken breast or thigh (the recipe's own suggested economical protein) — roughly halves the fat while keeping protein as high or higher

Cut the flash-fry oil to a thin film instead of enough to submerge — the velveting marinade (baking soda + cornstarch + egg white) already does most of the tenderizing work, so less oil is needed to get a good result
Use low-sodium soy sauce for both the marinade and the sauce
Halve the brown sugar — the Shaoxing wine and soy already bring plenty of flavor
Keep the capsicum — it's doing real nutritional work here (vitamin C)

her_preconception.verdict: Good iron from the beef and a solid vitamin-C boost from the capsicum and spring onion (which also helps absorb that iron — a nice pairing as written). Cook the beef fully through as standard. The downsides are the same as his: fairly high sodium and fat, and it's not a folate or choline source on its own. Shaoxing wine is a cooking wine — most of the alcohol cooks off during the simmer, but it's worth noting if she prefers to avoid it entirely; a swap exists.
prenatal_highlights: iron from beef, paired with vitamin C (capsicum, spring onion) for better absorption

safety_advisories.note: Shaoxing wine is a cooking wine — most alcohol cooks off during the simmer, but if she'd rather avoid any alcohol in the dish, there's a direct swap.
safety_advisories.swap: rice vinegar + a splash of chicken/beef stock in place of the Shaoxing wine

suggested_mods: Chicken breast swap (as for him) also helps her lens — less fat, same iron-absorption pairing with the capsicum
Use low-sodium soy; keep the capsicum for the vitamin C

cooking_guide: Slice the beef thin and AGAINST THE GRAIN — this is what keeps stir-fried beef tender rather than chewy; look for the direction of the muscle fibers and cut perpendicular to them.

The baking soda + cornstarch + egg white marinade is a classic Chinese 'velveting' technique — it tenderizes and forms a protective coating so the meat stays juicy through the hot flash-fry. Don't skip it, and don't over-marinate past the stated time or the texture can turn mushy.
If using the optional extra-tenderizing baking-soda step, rinse it off thoroughly and pat the meat fully dry before mixing in the actual marinade — any baking soda left on gives an off, soapy taste.
Dust lightly in cornstarch right before frying, not earlier — shake off the excess so you get a thin, crisp coating rather than a gummy one.
Flash-fry at a moderate 120-140°C (lower than a typical deep-fry) in small batches — crowding the pan drops the oil temperature and the coating steams instead of crisping.
Build the sauce in the same pan after the aromatics so it picks up the fond (browned bits) left behind — that's a lot of the flavor.
Toss the protein back in only at the very end, off or just over the heat, so the crisp coating doesn't go soggy sitting in the sauce too long.
Tip: for a lighter version, swap in chicken and shallow-fry in a thin film of oil rather than enough to submerge the pieces — the velveting marinade does most of the tenderizing work either way.
